evidence.note: 'actor-isolated state can change across an await ... developers must be sure not to break invariants across an await.'
TSPL: overlapping actor calls are not guaranteed idempotent; 'write them so they don't contain an await in the middle.'

swift-actor-reentrancy-stale-state.whyNotLinter: The compiler accepts reentrant actor code by design (it is data-race safe); whether a pre-await read is still valid is a question about intent. No SwiftLint rule covers it (rule directory checked).
swift-actor-reentrancy-stale-state.aiRelevance: High. Agents write the natural check-await-set shape (duplicate fetches, double submits, lost updates) and Swift 6 compiling cleanly makes them trust it. Grade: inference from how common the pattern is in cache/loader code; no controlled study found.
swift-actor-reentrancy-stale-state.expectedNoise: med — the question says the check and the dependent write must straddle an `await`; code that sets the flag before awaiting is a listed hard negative. The risk is snippets where the actor context isn't visible.

evidence.note: 'Only use nonisolated(unsafe) when you are carefully guarding all access to the variable with an external synchronization mechanism'; @unchecked Sendable is for types 'already doing manual synchronization'.
Blog (2026-06-29): coding agent added @unchecked Sendable to make a data-race error disappear; tests stayed green. Lead only.

swift-unchecked-sendable-unsynchronized.whyNotLinter: The compiler deliberately stops checking once these annotations are present. SwiftLint has only `redundant_sendable` and `incompatible_concurrency_annotation` (opt-in), neither of which asks whether the state is actually synchronized. A regex ban on `@unchecked` would also flag correct lock-protected types.
swift-unchecked-sendable-unsynchronized.aiRelevance: High. When a build fails under Swift 6, the shortest way to green is adding `@unchecked Sendable` or `nonisolated(unsafe)`, and agents take it (D-grade reports; plausible given how often these annotations show up in pre-2024 training code).
swift-unchecked-sendable-unsynchronized.expectedNoise: low — correct uses almost always show the lock or queue right next to the state, and the question requires that it be absent.
swift-unchecked-sendable-unsynchronized.evidenceStatus: single official B source for the exact API; needs a second B (or A from a repo) before shipping as built-in, or accept it on the strength of the vendor doc

evidence.note: 'If the task is canceled before the time ends, this function throws CancellationError.'
TSPL 'Task Cancellation': tasks must check cancellation cooperatively with Task.checkCancellation() or Task.isCancelled.

swift-cancellation-swallowed-in-loop.whyNotLinter: `try?` on a throwing call is legal and often right. Whether it sits in a loop that depends on the thrown error to stop is a judgment about control flow and intent. No SwiftLint rule covers it.
swift-cancellation-swallowed-in-loop.aiRelevance: High. Agents write `while true { await refresh(); try? await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(30)) }` polling loops in `.task` or view models because `try?` is the quickest way to satisfy `throws`.
swift-cancellation-swallowed-in-loop.expectedNoise: low — the shape (a loop containing `try?` + sleep with no cancellation check) is narrow, and the listed negatives cover the correct variants.

evidence.note: 'an unstructured task doesn't have a parent task ... you're also completely responsible for their correctness.'
Migration guide shows task groups with bounded child tasks as the way to fan out work.

swift-unstructured-task-in-async-context.whyNotLinter: `Task { }` is legal everywhere and right in synchronous entry points. Whether the caller is already async and could await, or whether the task is tracked elsewhere, takes judgment. SwiftLint `unhandled_throwing_task` (opt-in) only covers throwing bodies whose error is dropped.
swift-unstructured-task-in-async-context.aiRelevance: High. Agents bring GCD-era habits into async code (`for x in xs { Task { await upload(x) } }`) and wrap awaits in `Task { }` to get around 'async call in a function that does not support concurrency' errors, even when the caller is already async.
swift-unstructured-task-in-async-context.expectedNoise: med — synchronous entry points look similar; the `false` list names them explicitly.

evidence.note: The canonical callback-adaptation example 'Sets the continuation's onTermination property to a closure that calls stopMonitoring()'.

swift-asyncstream-missing-ontermination.whyNotLinter: Whether the producer is long-lived and needs teardown depends on what it is (observer vs. fixed values). No SwiftLint rule or compiler diagnostic covers it.
swift-asyncstream-missing-ontermination.aiRelevance: Medium-high. Agents often wrap NotificationCenter or delegate APIs in AsyncStream and yield from the callback but leave out onTermination. Grade: inference; it is the same teardown gap as the existing continuation-cancellation rule.
swift-asyncstream-missing-ontermination.expectedNoise: low — the rule only fires when a long-lived producer is visible and onTermination is missing.
swift-asyncstream-missing-ontermination.evidenceStatus: single official B source for the exact API; needs a second B (or A from a repo) before shipping as built-in, or accept it on the strength of the vendor doc

evidence.note: 'When any of the cars change name, the onChange closure is then called on the first change.'
Observations async sequence exists for tracking ongoing changes.

swift-observation-tracking-one-shot.whyNotLinter: Whether the caller wants one notification or all of them is intent. The API compiles either way.
swift-observation-tracking-one-shot.aiRelevance: Medium. The name reads like a subscription, so agents treat it as one. Volume is low because few edits call this API; each hit is a real bug.
swift-observation-tracking-one-shot.expectedNoise: low — rare API, and correct uses show the recursive re-arm.

evidence.note: 'A State property always instantiates its default value when SwiftUI instantiates the view. For this reason, avoid side effects and performance-intensive work when initializing the default value.' The same guidance appears on the Xcode 27 State() macro page.

swiftui-state-default-heavy-init.whyNotLinter: Whether an initializer is cheap or does I/O is a judgment about what the call does. SwiftLint `private_swiftui_state` only checks access control.
swiftui-state-default-heavy-init.aiRelevance: High during Observation migrations. Agents mechanically replace `@StateObject var x = X()` (lazy autoclosure) with `@State var x = X()` (eager), which moves side-effecting initializers onto every view init.
swiftui-state-default-heavy-init.expectedNoise: med — the snippet often doesn't show what an initializer does; the question limits it to side effects visible as written, and plain `Model()` is a listed negative.
swiftui-state-default-heavy-init.evidenceStatus: single official B source for the exact API; needs a second B (or A from a repo) before shipping as built-in, or accept it on the strength of the vendor doc
